content.text: Chapter Six
Deatholme's Price
The first undead reached the archive before they reached the ossuary stairs.

Lethira heard them beyond the eastern door and raised a closed fist. Four sets of boots stopped among torn ledgers, extinguished runes, and bodies emptied of more than life. The alarm passed through the walls in slow crimson pulses. Each one pulled Rynel’s attention toward the buried anchor beneath the ruined table.

Falanaras watched the captain’s chin turn a fraction before discipline caught it. Rynel’s shoulders remained hunched. The flesh beneath his eyes had drawn tight enough to show every sleepless hour, and his right hand kept closing around the memory of power.
“How many?” Rynel asked.
Lethira knelt beside the door. “Six dragging their feet. One trying very hard to remember how.”

“Ghouls and a necromancer,” Theron said. He shifted the heavier shield against his arm. Blood had spread beyond the fresh binding at his ribs, though he stood without leaning on the table. “The eastern passage?”

Falanaras consulted the narrow plan. The archive’s eastern door opened toward a service hall that crossed the ossuary stairs. The command register lay below them. Their withdrawal route began farther east, beyond a primary anchor set beneath an old gatehouse.
“We need that hall,” he said.

Rynel pointed toward the overturned table. “Dawnspear, bind the ledgers. Brightshield, door. Valeflame, take the necromancer when it enters.” His voice rasped, yet the orders came in the old sequence, each name receiving a task before danger could become confusion. “Call every draw. Mine first.”
Lethira’s eyes rested on his hooked fingers. “And if you do not stop?”
For one heartbeat, shame made him look older than hunger had. “Stop me.”

Falanaras threaded the ledger chains through his belt and tightened the straps of his pack over the Sunstrider message case. The lacquered weight pressed between his shoulder blades. Rynel’s summons had passed into his keeping on the road; now the captain carried only his glaive and the ruin he had made of himself.
The eastern door burst inward.

Theron caught it on his shield and drove forward. The first ghoul struck the iron face hard enough to break its jaw. Lethira’s arrow passed over his shoulder and entered the eye of the robed corpse behind it. The necromancer’s crooked staff fell before the violet spark gathering at its tip could become a spell.

Rynel killed the second ghoul with the inner edge of his glaive. The third came low. He turned the haft, broke its forearm, and stamped its skull against the threshold. Every movement belonged to the captain Falanaras knew. Only the pause afterward betrayed him: his gaze fixed on the dead necromancer’s staff, where the interrupted spark still trembled.
“Rynel.” Falanaras used his name before the distance widened.
The captain struck the staff with his boot. Its crystal rolled beneath a shelf and went dark. “Move.”

They crossed the service hall before another patrol answered the alarm. Ossuary niches climbed the walls around the descending stair, their contents long since pulled out and given weapons. A chain ran down the center rail. Every few breaths it jerked by itself, carrying the alarm deeper into the earth.

Lethira cut the chain at the first landing. The severed links lashed the stone and stilled. Above them, ghouls poured into the archive they had abandoned. Their claws scraped across the fallen deathguard and the emptied acolytes. One began shrieking over what Rynel had left behind.

The stairs ended at a gallery beneath the foundations. Blue tile remained on portions of the floor, faded remnants of the elven hall that had stood there before Deatholme. The Scourge had cut channels through it and filled them with black resin. Red light traveled along those channels toward an iron door at the far end.
Falanaras crouched over the nearest line. Symbols for gates, patrol routes, and grave pits repeated inside the current. “The archive is ahead. The network is changing the eastern route.”
“Because it knows where we are?” Theron asked.

“Because it knows where the first anchor failed. It is closing every route attached to it.” Falanaras followed the current with the crescent of his glaive held a finger’s width above the floor. “If we take the register, we can identify which line controls the eastern gate.”

A pulse swept through the gallery. Rynel folded around it. His glaive struck the tile, and both hands locked on the haft as though it were the only fixed thing in the corridor. The resin brightened under his boots.

Falanaras moved between him and the channel. Rynel’s eyes rose to his face slowly. Hunger had pared away the reserve behind them. For an instant he looked ready to shove Falanaras aside and go down on his knees over the current.
“Give me a crystal,” Rynel said.

Falanaras removed one from his pouch. He kept it in his own palm while Rynel drew. The measured light thinned at once. When the captain’s fingers closed over Falanaras’s wrist and tried to pull the crystal nearer, Theron set the rim of his shield against Rynel’s forearm.
“Three,” Theron said.
Rynel stared at the remaining glow. The tremor moved from his jaw into his hand. Then he released Falanaras and stepped back.
“Three,” he agreed.
No one pretended the number meant what it had on the road.

The iron door had no handle. Nine command sigils covered its face, linked by thin strands of necromantic fire. Falanaras recognized five from the copied ward sequence and two from the ledgers hanging at his belt. The remaining pair changed whenever he tried to hold them in his sight.
“It expects an order from the network,” he said. “I can imitate one, but the alarm will challenge it.”
Rynel lowered his glaive across the corridor. “Then answer faster than it asks.”

Falanaras set his palm against the first sigil. Cold entered his bones. He caught the command running beneath the iron, turned it, and spoke the opening sequence through his glaive. One sigil dimmed. Three others flared in challenge. He answered from the ledger. Behind them, the cut alarm chain began hammering against the stair rail again.

The last pair shifted. Falanaras drove the point of his weapon between them and forced their current apart. The door opened the width of a hand. Theron wedged his shield into the gap and heaved until ancient hinges tore free of the wall.

The control archive smelled of wax, old blood, and earth opened too long from the sun. Shelves held iron cylinders stamped with the names of ruined settlements. At the center stood a lectern built around a slab of dark stone. A register lay chained upon it, its pages made from thin gray hide and edged in brass.

A figure waited behind the lectern. It had once been an elf. The remnants of a magister’s mantle hung from one shoulder, and silver wire held its split skull together. Both hands had been replaced with bundles of black quills that scratched orders across separate sheets without pause.
It looked at Rynel first.
“Open vessel,” it whispered in Thalassian. “Come closer.”
Rynel’s whole body tightened. The quills rose. Green-black fire ran from their tips through the brass edges of the register, offering a concentrated current stronger than the one beneath the floor.

Lethira’s arrow struck the creature through the mouth. It staggered, quills flinging ink across the shelves. Rynel did not reach for the magic. He brought his glaive down on the lectern instead, severing the nearest conduit before the offered current touched him.

The undead scribe screamed around the arrow. Sheets rose from every table and folded into cutting wings. Theron covered Falanaras while paper blades rang against his shield. Lethira vaulted a low shelf and drove her knife into the silver wire at the back of the scribe’s skull.

Falanaras hooked the register’s chain with his glaive. The first pull drew fire up the haft and opened both burned palms. He reversed the current, caught the locking spell at its hinge, and sent it into the broken lectern. Brass links burst across the floor.
Rynel killed the scribe with one thrust beneath the ribs. The magic inside it rushed toward the wound. His hand jerked open. Falanaras saw the choice arrive before the captain made it.
Rynel wrenched his weapon free and stepped away. The scribe collapsed with its power still guttering through the quills.
“Take it,” he said.

Falanaras wrapped the register in the dead reader’s mantle and secured it beneath his pack straps. Lethira swept the shelves for route cylinders while Theron braced the ruined door. The first impact from outside bent his wounded arm and drove a cry through his teeth.
“Eastern gate,” Falanaras said, reading the opened page. “The primary anchor controls a descending barrier and three side passages. There is a service stair beyond it leading to the outer trench.”
“Then we have what we came for,” Rynel said. “Withdraw.”
They left through a records chute behind the shelves while Scourge forces battered down the main door.

The chute dropped them into a passage so narrow Theron had to turn his shield sideways. Rynel went last. Falanaras heard him breathing behind the scrape of armor, each exhale rougher than the one before it. When the archive door finally failed, the captain severed a ceiling brace and sent stone crashing into the chute mouth.
The collapse bought them minutes. Deatholme spent them well.

At the next junction, the route marked open in the register ended behind a wall of red force. Falanaras found a secondary line and led them through a burial chamber where corpses stood packed upright in salt. Half woke as the blood elves passed. Lethira cut their binding cords, and the reanimated corpses fell against one another before they could raise their weapons.
Theron’s wound opened fully on the climb beyond. He left a dark print whenever his right hand touched the wall. Falanaras offered to take the shield. Theron shook his head.
“You have the register, the prince, and our captain’s better judgment in your pack,” he said. “I will carry one ugly piece of iron.”
“My better judgment is walking,” Rynel said from behind them.
Theron glanced back. “That explains the pace.”

The answer might once have earned the smallest movement at the corner of Rynel’s mouth. Now his gaze had fixed on the red barrier behind them. Power ran through it in heavy waves. He followed until Lethira stepped into his line of sight.
“The exit is this way,” she said.
He looked at her as though returning from a long distance. “I know.”

The primary anchor announced itself before they saw it. The passage vibrated under their boots. Dust rose from the joints between stones, and the hunger sharpened inside Falanaras until his tongue felt too large for his mouth. Ahead, pale daylight showed through an arched gate crossed by a curtain of red-black fire.

The anchor stood in a recess beside the arch: a waist-high pillar of black stone bound with iron bands. Threads entered it from the walls and emerged as one thick current feeding the barrier. Beyond the gate, a descending stair turned toward the eastern trench and freedom.
Lethira reached the opening first. She stopped so abruptly Falanaras nearly struck her.

Scourge waited in the side galleries. Armored corpses filled both approaches, shields locked beneath hanging cages. Two acolytes stood behind them with their hands joined around a suspended shard of sickly crystal. The alarm had not driven the garrison toward the intruders. It had driven them here.
“Ambush,” Lethira said, already loosing.
Her arrow struck an acolyte’s joined hands. The shard dropped. Both shield lines advanced.

Theron met the left line at the mouth of the passage. Falanaras took the right. A necromantic working hardened the first corpse’s spear arm and drove the weapon toward him with strength dead muscle did not possess. He caught the spearhead on the crescent of his glaive, peeled the strengthening enchantment from the rune behind it, and cast the stolen force across to Theron. Green-black light tightened around Theron’s shield arm. He broke the left line’s first rank with a single shove. Rynel entered between them. His weapon cut once across a corpse’s throat, reversed, and split another helm to the brow.

The second acolyte raised the fallen shard. Necromantic force gathered above the formation in a dark, turning mass. Falanaras reached for it with his spellbreaker training and found the anchor already holding every strand. The attack and the barrier were one working. Breaking either carelessly would bring the gate down upon them.
“Anchor!” he shouted. “It controls the strike.”
Rynel turned toward the pillar. The concentrated current lit his face from below. His pupils narrowed. His free hand rose before he seemed aware of it.
The dark mass fell.

Rynel caught the falling mass on the runes of his glaive. The hostile working pressed for his flesh and found no easy hold; its force drove him to one knee instead. He drew a hard, measured mouthful from the leading edge, thinning the spell enough to move beneath it. Then he set the crescent against the descending weight and wrenched its physical course sideways. The dark mass crashed into the locked shields. Corpses flew against the gallery wall. The crystal shard broke in the acolyte’s hands.
A spear came through the opened line and entered Rynel below the rear edge of his breastplate.

He made no sound. He trapped the shaft under one arm, dragged the corpse close, and opened its throat with the rear blade of his glaive. When he rose, the broken spearhead remained inside him. Blood ran beneath his armor and darkened his thigh.
“Captain,” Falanaras said.
“Finish the line.”

They did. Theron held the passage while Lethira killed the remaining acolyte. Falanaras broke the last command rune on the right-hand formation and released the magic into the floor. When the final corpse fell, fresh howls answered from behind them. The archive garrison had found another route through the collapse.

Rynel leaned against the anchor recess. He had become terribly still. The pillar pulsed beside his face, and every pulse reflected in his overbright eyes. His blood reached the floor in a steady thread.
Falanaras opened the register across Theron’s shield. “The barrier releases if the anchor receives a withdrawal command. It will close again when the network challenges it.”
“How long?” Lethira asked.
“Long enough for two, perhaps three. Someone has to keep turning the challenge away.”
Theron looked at Rynel’s wound. “We carry him.”
“You cannot carry yourself,” Rynel said.

He set his glaive against the anchor. Green-black fire climbed the blade. His body curved toward it with an eagerness that made Falanaras’s stomach turn. The power was enough to flood every empty place inside him, and the task required some of it. Beneath that abundance lay the ward’s simpler purpose: receive a withdrawal order, open the passage, reject any command the wider network did not confirm. Rynel closed his will around that purpose. The danger lay in whether he could seize the ward without surrendering to what fed it.

Rynel drew once. The current entered him in a bitter rush, and his shoulders pulled upright. Before relief could become pursuit, he closed his hand, set the weapon’s crescent across the flow, and guided the rest away from his skin.
The barrier shuddered open.
“Valeflame first,” he ordered. “Find the outer route. Brightshield follows.”
Lethira did not move. Her bow remained raised toward the rear passage, but her eyes were on him. “There is room for another hand on that weapon.”
“There is room for another corpse beside it.” Rynel’s arms shook as the network struck back. “I have filled that position.”

The approaching Scourge forces rounded the far junction. Theron stepped between them and the anchor, shield lifting despite the blood down his side. “Go,” he told Lethira. “I remain offensive to look at.”
She crossed with a curse sharp enough to serve as farewell. Theron backed through after her, catching one thrown blade on his shield before the barrier’s fire passed over his armor.
Falanaras stayed.

Rynel’s gaunt face tightened with effort. Each challenge from the network arrived as a completed order meant to close the barrier, burn the intruder from the anchor, or call the side passages shut. The runes on his armor and glaive kept those hostile commands from fastening directly to him. He skimmed only enough power to hold his wounded body upright, caught each rejected instruction where it returned to the anchor, and forced it into another branch of the same ward network: the closing command into an empty side gate, the burning current into a ceiling conduit, the pressure meant to crush his body through the floor channel beneath the Scourge advancing along the passage. Sweat and blood ran together beneath his gorget.
“I can hold it,” Falanaras said. “You cross. We trade from the other side.”
“You cannot hold this and the register.”
“Then we leave the register.”
“No.” The word held the same finality with which Rynel had once ordered recruits away from a failing wall. “You said I was fit to move. This is where I moved.”

The rebuke entered exactly where Falanaras’s guilt had been waiting. He had chosen the objective after seeing what Rynel had become. He could blame rank, urgency, or the captain’s remaining usefulness. None of them altered the choice.
Rynel’s eyes shifted to the pack on Falanaras’s shoulders. “The prince asked for an officer. He will receive one.”
Falanaras shook his head. “Halduron decides that.”
“Halduron will complain that I made his decision untidy.” A broken breath might have been a laugh. “Then he will make it.”

The undead were ten paces away. Rynel turned another strike into the side wall. Stone burst outward, and his knees nearly failed. The anchor’s light flooded the hollows of his face, offering more than the failing body could use. His mouth tightened. His hand did not open again.
“Captain,” Falanaras said.
Rynel looked at him. For the first time since the vault, his gaze did not slip toward any light. “Take them home. Answer the summons. Those are my last orders, Dawnspear.”
Falanaras crossed the barrier.

On the far side, Theron caught his pack and dragged him down the stair. Lethira stood three steps below with an arrow drawn past her cheek. Rynel remained visible through the red-black curtain, bent over his glaive while the Scourge closed around the anchor recess.

He shifted his weapon from controlling the ward to striking its source. The crescent bit through the anchor’s iron band. Every remaining current met the blade at once. Rynel tore power out through the fracture, and the magical loss became damage inside the stone. Cracks raced down the pillar toward the gatehouse foundations.
The anchor split.

White-green fire filled the arch. The barrier vanished, followed by the ceiling above it. Falanaras saw Rynel once within the glare—upright despite the spear wound, both hands on the glaive, face set toward the collapsing passage while power tore free around him. Then the gatehouse came down.

The collapse threw all three survivors down the stair. Stone struck Falanaras’s shoulder and tore the register loose. He caught its wrapping before it slid into the dust. Behind them, the passage disappeared under iron, rock, and bodies.
Lethira climbed toward the rubble.
Theron caught the back of her harness. “No.”

She twisted hard enough to open his wound further. He held on. Dust rolled through the stairwell and covered them both in gray. Somewhere beyond the collapse, Deatholme’s linked wards began failing one after another. Each rupture sounded like distant thunder under the earth.
Falanaras heard Rynel’s order inside the noise.
“We move,” he said.
Lethira looked at him with murder in her face. Then she tore free of Theron, turned, and led them down toward the trench.
The service stair ended behind a grate overlooking Deatholme’s eastern ditch. Lethira forced the rusted latch with her knife. Cold rain struck their faces as they crawled out beneath the wall.

The stronghold had turned upon itself. One tower’s ward-flames burned without fuel; another had gone completely dark. Ghouls crowded gates that no longer recognized them. Commands raced along broken anchor lines and returned changed, sending patrols toward empty courtyards while the three blood elves crossed the ditch below.

They reached the blighted trees before pursuit found the correct gate. Lethira chose no trail. She moved by root, fallen trunk, and the memory of ground seen only once. Theron lasted half a mile before his shield slipped from his hand.
Falanaras took it then. Lethira took Theron’s other arm. Between them they carried him north while Deatholme’s horns sounded through the rain.

At dawn they hid beneath the roots of a fallen tree. Theron drifted in and out while Lethira rebound his side with a strip cut from her cloak. Falanaras sat at the mouth of the hollow with the register against his chest and Rynel’s glaive absent from the weapons beside him.

He could still see the captain taking a measured current from the anchor and closing his hand while power remained. The image demanded meaning. Sacrifice offered the easiest one, and Falanaras distrusted ease. Rynel had concealed his hunger, endangered the mission, emptied the acolytes, and raised magic against him. His last choice erased none of it.
It remained his choice.

When the anchor opened itself to him, Rynel had taken what their survival required and stopped before need became surrender. He had spent the power on their lives and paid with his own. Falanaras could honor that without pretending the road to it had been noble.
Lethira tied off Theron’s bandage. “If you make him a saint, I will shoot you.”
Falanaras looked at her. She kept her eyes on the knot.
“I was not,” he said.
“Good.” Her hands shook once after she finished. “He would have hated the promotion.”
Theron opened one eye. “He hated most things done badly.”
They rested until the horns faded. Then they continued north.

Farstrider scouts found them near the first surviving Eversong ward. The green haze thinned above the road. Gold leaves appeared among bare branches, so bright after Deatholme that Falanaras could not look at them for long.

Halduron met them inside the gate of the forward post. His attention counted three before it touched the register in Falanaras’s arms. He did not ask where Rynel was until healers had taken Theron and a ranger had closed the gate behind Lethira.
“Report,” he said.

Falanaras gave him everything. He described the vault, Rynel’s uncontrolled feeding, the command register, the eastern ambush, the spear wound, and the anchor. He did not soften the moment when Rynel turned on him. He did not improve the captain’s final words.
Halduron listened without interruption. Rain ticked against the command lodge windows. The same border map lay across the table, now crowded with markers taken from the register’s first pages.
“He told you to answer the summons,” Halduron said when Falanaras finished.
“Yes.”
“And you crossed.”
Falanaras felt the rubble fall again. “Yes.”

Halduron closed the register. “Then do not make his order smaller by wishing you had disobeyed it.” His expression hardened before the words could become comfort. “You should have withdrawn after the vault. Rynel was unfit, Brightshield was wounded, and you knew both facts. The intelligence may save every patrol between here and the Scar. That does not make your decision wise.”
“No, Ranger-General.”

“You will write that in your formal account. You will also write why you continued. Command requires both.” Halduron touched the Sunstrider case where Falanaras had placed it beside the register. “The company gathers in Silvermoon in five days. Rynel’s place remains requested.”
Falanaras waited.

“Captain Starweaver made a field recommendation,” Halduron said. “I am choosing to accept it. Effective immediately, you hold his rank and his remaining command. Silvermoon will confirm the appointment before you depart.”
The title did not feel like elevation. It settled over Falanaras with the weight of a dead man’s armor, still warm where another body had worn it.
“Understood,” he said.
Silvermoon confirmed the promotion beneath a roof Rynel had helped defend.

There was no ceremony beyond a clerk, a sealed order, and Halduron fastening a captain’s insignia to Falanaras’s formal mantle. The room overlooked a rebuilt avenue where workers were raising another crystal into place. Its green light entered through the tall windows and caught on the metal at his throat.

The recovered register had already changed the Ghostlands war. Two anchor sites were destroyed before Deatholme could relocate them. A missing patrol was found alive behind a warded ravine. Halduron listed those results without suggesting they balanced a life.

Afterward, Falanaras found Theron and Lethira on a western terrace above the military quarter. Theron had exchanged field bindings for a rigid brace and leaned against the balustrade with great dignity. Lethira wore Serenya’s black-fletched arrow in her quiver among the red and gold of Silvermoon.
She looked at the insignia. “That was quick. Did they run out of better candidates?”
“One,” Theron said.
Silence followed. It was brief, which made it bearable.
Falanaras placed the departure order on the balustrade. “I report to the southern quay before dawn. The company sails with the next tide.”
Lethira read the names below his assignment. “Liadrin. Rommath. Astalor Bloodsworn.” Her brow rose. “You have found an efficient way to become the least important person in any room.”
“He has practiced,” Theron said.

Falanaras folded the order again. Beyond the terrace, the western quarter remained open to the sky where House Dawnspear had stood. Farther south lay the Ghostlands, Deatholme, and a grave they could not recover. Beyond all of them waited Outland and the prince whose summons had reached into Rynel’s last hours.
“Edric crossed our border,” he said. “Serenya helped hold it. Rynel died inside the place we were trying to take back. I leave tomorrow, and none of it feels connected.”
Theron looked south. “It will. Usually at an inconvenient time.”
Lethira removed the black arrow from her quiver and turned it once between her fingers. “If the prince has found salvation, ask whether it comes with competent border policy.”
“I will include it after the military questions.”

Theron held out his hand. Falanaras clasped his forearm carefully above the brace. Lethira refused any gesture that could be named farewell and adjusted the new insignia where Halduron had set it crooked.
“There,” she said. “Now you may disgrace the rank on your own.”

They remained on the terrace until the western light failed. Below them, Silvermoon’s wards brightened one by one. Falanaras felt each source as a quiet pressure behind his teeth. None drew his gaze away from his friends.
Before dawn, he would carry Rynel’s summons south.
The captain who had received it remained beneath Deatholme. The captain who answered would have to decide what that inheritance required.
